entries.label: Lists only some of the outcomes that give the wanted result
entries.description: The student writes down one or two outcomes that give the wanted result, such as a total of 8, and treats that as the whole event set, leaving out the other outcomes that also give it.
entries.signal: The event set for a total of 8 with two dice holds only some of the pairs, for example just (4, 4), or just (2, 6) and (6, 2).

refutation.text_md: The pairs you wrote really do total 8, so that part is right. The slip is stopping there: an event is not one outcome you spotted, it is the whole set of outcomes you are interested in.

The learner is hoping for a total of 8, so every outcome that gives 8 counts. Take the outcome where the first die shows 3 and the second shows 5. It totals 8, so it belongs to the event, but it is missing from a set that holds only $(4, 4)$, and from a set that holds only $(2, 6)$ and $(6, 2)$.
The same thing happens with a pack of cards that has had the clubs taken out. The event of drawing a picture card is every J, Q and K of hearts, diamonds and spades, not just one of those cards.
Go through the pairs the two dice can show and keep every one whose total is 8. That gives the event set $\{(2, 6), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 3), (6, 2)\}$.

entries.label: Picks the sample space of a different experiment
entries.description: The student chooses a set they remember from another experiment, such as heads and tails from a coin toss, without checking that it lists the results of the experiment actually described.
entries.signal: The sample space given for a die roll is $\{H, T\}$, or any list whose members a die cannot show.

refutation.text_md: $\{H, T\}$ really is a sample space, for tossing a coin, where the results are heads and tails. The mix-up is matching the set to a familiar example instead of to the experiment in front of you.

A sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of the experiment, so it has to be built from this experiment. Here a die is rolled. Ask of each member of the set: can the die show this? A die can never land on $H$ or $T$.
What a die can land on is the numbers on its faces. Heads and tails would only belong in the sample space if a coin were being tossed.

Before choosing, say the experiment in your own words, here a die is rolled. Then list every result that experiment can give, and check that each member of your set could really happen. For a die that is $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$.

entries.label: Gives an event in place of the sample space
entries.description: The student writes a set picked out by a condition, such as only the odd numbers on a die, when the sample space is every possible outcome of the experiment.
entries.signal: The sample space given for a single die roll leaves out some of the numbers 1 to 6, for example $\{1, 3, 5\}$.

refutation.text_md: $\{1, 3, 5\}$ is a perfectly good set: it is the odd numbers a die can show. The mix-up is between an event, which is a set of outcomes you are interested in, and the sample space, which is every possible outcome.
Test it. If the die lands on 4, that is a possible outcome of the experiment, but it is not in $\{1, 3, 5\}$. A sample space must hold every possible outcome, so it cannot leave out 2, 4 or 6.

A pack of cards with the clubs taken out shows the split. The sample space is every card left in the pack, while the event of drawing a picture card is only the J, Q and K of hearts, diamonds and spades.

To write a sample space, do not filter. Ask what the experiment could give and list all of it, which for a die is $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$. Keep a smaller set like $\{1, 3, 5\}$ for when you are told you are interested in only some of the results.

entries.label: Treats outcomes that are not equally likely as if they were
entries.description: The student counts the kinds of result (for example the colours in a bag) as the outcomes and divides by that count, or applies n(E)/n(S) to a situation whose outcomes are not equally likely.
entries.signal: Gives 1 over the number of categories, such as $\frac{1}{4}$ for a red ball from a bag of four colours, instead of using the number of balls.

refutation.text_md: It is natural to list the different things that could happen, for example four colours in a bag, and take $n(S)=4$ so that $P(\text{red})=\frac{1}{4}$. Listing the possible results is the right first move, and the formula $P(E)=\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}$ is the right formula. The catch is what you are allowed to count.
$P(E)=\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}$ only works when every outcome counted in $n(S)$ is equally likely.

Test it on a bag with $6$ red balls, $3$ blue balls, $2$ green balls and $1$ white ball. Is picking red as likely as picking white? There are six red balls and only one white one, so no. The four colours are not equally likely outcomes, so $\frac{1}{4}$ cannot be the probability of red.

What is equally likely is each individual ball: any one ball is as likely to be picked as any other. So $n(S)=12$ balls and $n(E)=6$ red balls, which gives $P(\text{red})=\frac{6}{12}=\frac{1}{2}$. That is different from $\frac{1}{4}$, and it matches the fact that half the balls are red.

The same warning applies beyond bags. The possible final scores of a soccer match are not all equally likely, so $\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}$ cannot be used to find the probability of a team winning. This method does not apply there.

Before you count, ask: is each outcome I am counting as likely as every other one? If yes, use $\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}$. If you listed kinds or categories that are not equally likely, count the outcomes that are, such as each ball rather than each colour, and write $n(E)$ and $n(S)$ from those.

entries.label: Gives a fixed 'expected' value instead of the fraction the trials produced
entries.description: The student treats the relative frequency of an event as one set number, such as 0.5 for heads, and gives that instead of working out the number of trials in which the event occurred divided by the total number of trials, or asks why the answer is not the same every time.

refutation.text_md: It is natural to feel that a coin has one 'right' answer for heads, such as $0.5$, and to give that whatever the question says happened. Counting heads is exactly the right idea; the slip is putting a number you expect in place of the number the trials gave.

A relative frequency is experimental. It is worked out only from the trials that were actually carried out: the number of trials in which the event occurs, divided by the total number of trials, $f=\frac{p}{t}$.

Compare two coin experiments. A coin tossed $30$ times lands on heads $17$ times, so $f=\frac{17}{30}=0.57$. A coin tossed $44$ times lands on heads $22$ times, so $f=\frac{22}{44}=0.50$. It is the same event with two different relative frequencies, and both are right because each one comes from its own trials.

That is why the book warns that a different relative frequency is possible every time the experiment is repeated: the value depends on the outcomes observed in that run. If you always answered $0.5$, the first coin would be marked wrong, because its trials gave $0.57$.
So read the question for two numbers only: how many trials had the event ($p$) and how many trials there were in all ($t$). Then calculate $\frac{p}{t}$ and round as the question asks.

entries.label: Reads only the part both circles share
entries.description: The student lists only the elements that sit inside both circles, as if the event set were just the shared part rather than everything inside its own circle.
entries.signal: The answer is a smaller set made up only of elements that lie in both circles; it leaves out elements that lie inside the named circle alone.

refutation.text_md: You found numbers that really do belong to the event, and none of them is wrong. The slip is stopping at the part the two circles share, as if the event set were only the shared numbers.
The event set of $A$ is every element inside circle $A$. A number inside both circles is inside circle $A$, so it counts, but a number inside circle $A$ and outside circle $B$ counts just the same.

For example, if circle $A$ holds twelve numbers and only $\{4, 7, 10, 14, 15\}$ of them are also in circle $B$, the other seven ($1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 11, 13$) sit in circle $A$ alone. They are still in the event, so the event set of $A$ is $\{1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15\}$, not just the shared five.
Shade the whole circle named in the question, including the part it shares with the other circle, then list every number inside the shaded part.

entries.label: Reads the other event's circle
entries.description: The student lists everything inside a circle, shared elements included, but it is the circle of the other event, not the one the question names.
entries.signal: The answer is exactly everything inside the other circle, so it contains an element that lies only in the other circle and misses elements that lie only in the named circle.

refutation.text_md: You read a circle the right way: you took every number inside it, shared ones included. The slip is which circle. The set you chose belongs to the other event, not the one the question names.
The letter in the question tells you which circle to read. Find the circle labelled with that letter first, before you read any numbers.

Here is a check that always works: take any number from your answer and ask whether it is inside the circle named in the question. If the question asks for the event set of $A$ and your answer contains a number such as 3 that sits inside circle $B$ only, that number is not in $A$, so the set cannot be the event set of $A$.
Read the letter in the question, find that circle, and list every number inside it, shared ones included.

entries.label: Reads the numbers outside the circle
entries.description: The student lists the elements that lie outside the circle for the event, instead of the elements inside it.
entries.signal: The answer is made up only of numbers of the sample space that are not inside the circle named in the question, so it contains none of the numbers inside that circle.

refutation.text_md: You separated the numbers inside the circle from the numbers outside it correctly. The slip is which group you kept: you listed the numbers outside the circle, and the event set is the numbers inside it.

An event set contains the elements that belong to the event, and those are the ones inside its circle. A number outside the circle does not belong to the event, whether it sits in the other circle or outside both circles.

For example, take the sample space of whole numbers from 1 to 15, and suppose only $\{3, 8, 12\}$ lie outside circle $A$. Those three are exactly the numbers that are not in the event. The other twelve are inside circle $A$, so the event set of $A$ has twelve elements, not three.
Find the circle named in the question and list the numbers inside it. Leave out everything outside that circle.

entries.label: Lists only the part of A that is outside B
entries.description: The student reads $A\cup B$ as just the first set and writes down only the elements that are in $A$ but not in $B$, leaving out the overlap and everything in $B$.
entries.signal: The answer lists only the elements of $A$ that are not also in $B$.

refutation.text_md: You went to set $A$ and wrote down the numbers in the part of $A$ that is outside $B$. Looking in $A$ is the right start, because everything in $A$ belongs to the union. The slip is stopping there, as if $A\cup B$ meant just $A$.
The circle for $A$ also contains the overlap. Those numbers are in $A$ as well as in $B$, so they belong to the union, and your list leaves them out.

Set $B$ has to be counted too: a number in $B$ is in "$A$ or $B$" even when it is not in $A$. Take a diagram where 1, 6, 7, 10 and 15 are in $A$ only, 8 is in $B$ only, and the overlap holds 2, 4, 5, 9, 11, 12, 13 and 14. A list of just 1, 6, 7, 10 and 15 has five numbers, but the union has fourteen, so it misses nine of them.

The move that works: shade the whole of $A$ and the whole of $B$, overlap included, then write down every number in the shaded part. A number is in the union when it is in at least one of the two sets.

entries.label: Takes only the overlap as the union
entries.description: The student writes down only the elements that are in both sets, the overlap of the two circles, as if $A\cup B$ meant "$A$ and $B$" instead of "$A$ or $B$".
entries.signal: The answer is a short list made up of the numbers in the overlap of the two circles.

refutation.text_md: You went to the overlap of the two circles, where the numbers are in both $A$ and $B$. Those numbers do belong to the union, so that was a sensible place to look. The slip is stopping there.
The union is "$A$ or $B$": a number only has to be in at least one of the two sets. Being in both is more than the union asks for. A number in $A$ alone qualifies, and so does a number in $B$ alone.

Check it on a diagram where 1, 6, 7, 10 and 15 are in $A$ only, 8 is in $B$ only, and the overlap holds 2, 4, 5, 9, 11, 12, 13 and 14. The number 6 is in $A$, so it is in "$A$ or $B$", yet it is not in the overlap. The same goes for 8, which is in $B$. The overlap holds only eight of the fourteen numbers in the union.

The move that works: treat the overlap as one part of the answer, not the whole of it. Shade the whole of $A$ and the whole of $B$, then write down every number in the shading, whether it is in one set or in both.

entries.label: Picks the number outside both circles
entries.description: The student writes down the element that sits outside both circles, in the sample space but in neither $A$ nor $B$, instead of the elements inside the circles.
entries.signal: The answer is only the number or numbers that sit outside both circles.

refutation.text_md: You picked out the number that sits in the box but outside both circles. It is a real number in the diagram, but it is the one number the union leaves out, not the one it collects.
The union $A\cup B$ is every element that is in at least one of the two sets. A number outside both circles is in neither $A$ nor $B$, so it fails that test.

Take a diagram where the sample space is the numbers 1 to 15 and only 3 sits outside both circles. Every other number from 1 to 15 is in $A$, in $B$, or in both, so the union is all of them: 1 to 15 with 3 missing. The answer $\{3\}$ is the one number the union cannot contain.

The move that works: ignore what is outside and work inside the circles. Shade the whole of $A$ and the whole of $B$, then write down every number in the shading. Anything left unshaded is not part of $A\cup B$.

entries.label: Gives one whole event set instead of the shared elements
entries.description: The student writes out every element of one event set ($A$ or $B$) and calls that the intersection, instead of keeping only the elements that are also in the other set.
entries.signal: The answer is one event set listed in full: it contains the shared elements but also elements that belong to only one of the two sets.

refutation.text_md: You found the right numbers to start from: the shared elements are in your list, and you looked in the right place. The slip is writing out a whole event set ($B$, or $A$) and calling it $A\cap B$. A whole set holds every one of its elements, shared or not.
$A\cap B$ means only the elements that are in both $A$ and $B$. So a number has to pass two checks: it is in $A$, and it is in $B$. One check is not enough.

Try it on an example where $B$ is $\{7, 10, 11\}$ and $A$ also contains 7 and 10, along with other numbers. Check each number of $B$ against $A$. 7 is in $A$, so it stays. 10 is in $A$, so it stays. 11 is not in $A$, so it fails and is left out.

That leaves $A\cap B=\{7, 10\}$. The list $\{7, 10, 11\}$ is just $B$ with nothing removed, so it is not the intersection. The same goes for writing out all of $A$: numbers that sit only in $A$ fail the check for $B$.
Next time, take one event set and go through its elements one by one, asking "is it in the other set too?" Write down only the ones that get a yes. That list is $A\cap B$.

entries.label: Collects the elements from both circles, not just the shared ones
entries.description: The student gathers the elements of event set $A$ together with those of event set $B$, so numbers that are in only one of the sets end up in the answer for $A\cap B$.
entries.signal: The answer is a long list that contains elements found in $A$ alone and in $B$ alone, as well as the shared ones.

refutation.text_md: You looked at both event sets, and the shared numbers are in your list. The slip is reading $A\cap B$ as "everything in $A$ together with everything in $B$", so numbers from only one circle came along too.

$A\cap B$ means only the elements that are in both sets. A number that sits in just one circle is not in both. In the example where the shared numbers are 7 and 10, the number 11 is in $B$ but not in $A$, and numbers such as 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 9 are in $A$ but not in $B$. None of these belongs in $A\cap B$.
Check any number in your list with two questions: is it in $A$? Is it in $B$? Only 7 and 10 get two yes answers. That is why $A\cap B=\{7, 10\}$ and not the longer list.
Next time, for each number you are tempted to write down, ask both questions. Write down only the numbers that get two yes answers: those are the elements of $A\cap B$.

entries.label: Adds the two probabilities and forgets what is in both events
entries.description: The student finds P(A) and P(B) and adds them, without subtracting P(A∩B), so every outcome that lies in both events is counted twice.
entries.signal: The answer is exactly P(A) + P(B) even though the two events share at least one outcome, for example 17/52 for 'a diamond or a three'.

refutation.text_md: You added $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ and stopped there. Adding is the right way to start, because the union is made of everything in $A$ and everything in $B$. The catch is that an outcome sitting in both events has been counted twice.

Try it on a card drawn from an ordinary pack of $52$ cards, asking for a diamond or a three. There are $13$ diamonds and $4$ threes, so adding the probabilities gives $\frac{13}{52}+\frac{4}{52}=\frac{17}{52}$.

But the three of diamonds is one of the $13$ diamonds and also one of the $4$ threes, so the sum counted that card twice. Only $16$ different cards are a diamond or a three, and the answer is $\frac{16}{52}=\frac{4}{13}$, not $\frac{17}{52}$.

That is the reason the identity has a third term: $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$. The only card in both events is the three of diamonds, so $n(A\cap B)=1$ and $P(A\cap B)=\frac{1}{52}$. Then $\frac{13}{52}+\frac{4}{52}-\frac{1}{52}=\frac{16}{52}$.

Each time you work out $P(A)$ and $P(B)$, also look for what is in both events and work out $P(A\cap B)=\frac{n(A\cap B)}{n(S)}$, then subtract it. When $A\cap B$ is empty, as with the event sets $\{1,2,5,6\}$ and $\{3\}$ on a six-number sample space, $P(A\cap B)=0$ and the subtraction changes nothing. That is why adding alone gave the right answer there.

entries.label: Treats two possible results as events that can happen together
entries.description: The student sees that each event is a real possibility in the same set-up (orange juice and apple juice are both in the fridge, red velvet and vanilla are both in the packet) and calls the events not mutually exclusive, instead of asking whether one single pick can be in both events.

refutation.text_md: You noticed that both events are real possibilities: the cooldrink could be orange juice, and it could be apple juice. That is true, and it is worth noticing. But it is not what "mutually exclusive" asks.
The question is whether the two events can occur **at the same time**, that is, whether any outcome belongs to both event sets. Two events can both be possible and still never happen together.

Look at what is actually being done: just **one** item is chosen (one cooldrink, one cupcake). That one item has a single flavour. It cannot be orange juice and apple juice at once, and it cannot be red velvet and vanilla at once. No outcome is in both event sets, so the events are mutually exclusive.

Compare a case where the answer really is "not mutually exclusive": one card chosen from a deck, with the events "the card is red" and "the card is a picture card". There a single card can be in both events, and that is what makes them not mutually exclusive.

The move to use each time: picture the single pick or the single game, and ask "can this one result be in both events at once?" If nothing can, the events are mutually exclusive, even though each of them is possible on its own.

entries.label: Thinks mutually exclusive events must cover every outcome
entries.description: The student rejects two events as not mutually exclusive because some other outcome belongs to neither of them (a tie, a grape juice), as if mutually exclusive meant that the two events use up everything that can happen.

refutation.text_md: You spotted that winning and losing are not the only things that can happen: a tie is possible too, and a tie counts as neither a win nor a loss. That is correct. The slip is in thinking it changes the answer.
"Mutually exclusive" asks one thing: can the two events occur at the same time, so that some outcome is in both event sets? It does not ask whether the two events together cover every outcome.

A tie is in neither event set, and an outcome that is in neither set cannot be in both. The team cannot win and lose the same game at the same time, so no outcome is in both events. They are mutually exclusive.

The same is true of a fridge with orange, apple and grape juice. Grape juice is left over, but one cooldrink still cannot be both orange juice and apple juice, so those two events are mutually exclusive as well.
The move to use each time: ignore the leftover outcomes and look only at the two events you were given. Is there any outcome that is in both? If not, they are mutually exclusive.

entries.label: Takes events described in different ways as having nothing in common
entries.description: The student sees red and picture as two different kinds of description (a colour and a type of card), assumes a card cannot be both, and calls the events mutually exclusive without checking whether any card is in both event sets.
entries.signal: Answers "mutually exclusive" for events described by different features of the same object, such as a red card and a picture card.

refutation.text_md: You are treating "red" and "picture card" as two different kinds of thing, a colour and a type of card, so it feels as if a card must be one or the other. Events do not become mutually exclusive just because their descriptions sound different.
The test is whether the two events can occur at the same time, that is, whether any card is in both event sets. So go and look for one card that fits both descriptions.
There is one. Some picture cards are red: for example the king of hearts is a red card and it is also a picture card. A single card can be both a red card and a picture card.
Because that card is in both event sets, the events can occur at the same time. They are **not** mutually exclusive.

The move to use each time: try to build one outcome that fits both descriptions. If you can, the events are not mutually exclusive. If you honestly cannot, as with a single cooldrink that is orange juice and apple juice, they are mutually exclusive.

entries.label: Adds P(A) and P(B) without checking the events cannot both happen
entries.description: The student treats P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) as a rule that always works and adds the two probabilities without first asking whether one outcome could belong to both events.

refutation.text_md: You are right that an "or" question is answered by adding two probabilities, and that is exactly what these questions need. What is missing is a check. The rule $P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)$ is true for **mutually exclusive** events only, which means two events that cannot both happen on the same pick.

Here is why the check matters. Adding $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ counts every outcome that belongs to $A$ and every outcome that belongs to $B$. If one outcome belongs to both, it gets counted twice. The full form of the rule takes the double count off: $P(A\cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A\cap B)$, where $P(A\cap B)$ is the probability that both events happen together.

Now test it on a box with 24 purple blocks, 41 white blocks and 116 blocks in all. One block cannot be both purple and white, so $P(\text{purple}\cap\text{white}) = 0$. The subtraction takes away nothing, and what is left is $\frac{24}{116}+\frac{41}{116}$. The same is true of a nursery child aged 3 or 4: a child has only one age, so the two groups of children cannot overlap and you can add their counts.

So before you add, ask yourself: "Can one pick be both $A$ and $B$?" If the answer is no, the events are mutually exclusive and you add $P(A) + P(B)$. If the answer is yes, a plain sum is not enough, because the overlap term is not 0.

entries.label: Complement is only what lies outside every circle
entries.description: The student takes the complement of a single event to be just the numbers that sit outside all the circles in the diagram, so numbers that are in the other circle but not in the event get left out.
entries.signal: The answer for the complement of one event is exactly the numbers outside both circles, with the numbers that lie only in the other circle missing.

refutation.text_md: You took the complement to mean the numbers outside every circle. Those numbers are certainly not in $B$, so they do belong in $B'$, which means you have part of the answer right.
But $B'$ means every number of the sample space that is not in the event $B$. Only the circle for $B$ is the event, so a number that is in the other circle, $A$, but not in $B$ is also not in $B$.

Take the numbers 2 and 10. They sit in circle $A$ but outside circle $B$, so they are in $B'$. "Outside both circles" skips them, which is why $\{3, 4, 6, 11, 12\}$ falls short of $\{2, 3, 4, 6, 10, 11, 12\}$.
"Outside both circles" is the right region only when the event is $A \cup B$, because then both circles are part of the event.
Next time, shade the event first, then list every number of the sample space that is not shaded. For each number you list, ask: is it in the event? If it is not, it belongs in the complement.

entries.label: Lists numbers from inside the event instead of outside it
entries.description: The student writes down numbers that lie inside the event's circle or circles (the event itself, or part of it) instead of the numbers of the sample space that are not in the event.
entries.signal: Every number in the answer is a member of the event itself, all of it or part of it, and none comes from outside the event.

refutation.text_md: You found numbers that really are inside the event, so you read the circles correctly. The complement asks for the opposite: the numbers of the sample space that are not in the event.
An event and its complement have no number in common. Every number of the sample space is in the event or in the complement, never in both.
That gives a quick test. Take any number from your answer and ask whether it is in the event. If it is, it cannot be in the complement, so it has to come out.

For $(A \cup B)'$, for example, the numbers inside the circles make up $A \cup B$ itself. The complement is what is left of the sample space once those are taken away, which is the numbers outside both circles.
Next time, shade the event first, then list the numbers that are left unshaded in the sample space. Finish by checking that none of the numbers you listed is in the event.

entries.label: Looks at the overlap of the circles instead of the two events named
entries.description: The student sees that the circles for A and B overlap and answers 'no', instead of writing out the two events the question actually names (a union and its complement) and checking whether those two share a number.
entries.signal: Answers 'no' (not mutually exclusive) when asked about an event and its complement, for example $A\cup B$ and $(A\cup B)'$.

refutation.text_md: You noticed that the two circles overlap, and that is true: the middle region $A\cap B$ is not empty. The catch is that the question is not asking about $A$ and $B$. It names two other events, $A\cup B$ and its complement $(A\cup B)'$, and those are the two we must compare.
Write each event as a set of numbers. $A\cup B$ is every number that is in at least one circle, so it includes the overlap. $(A\cup B)'$ is every number in the sample space that is in neither circle.

So a number that is in a circle, overlap included, belongs to $A\cup B$ and cannot also belong to $(A\cup B)'$. Take the example where $(A\cup B)'=\{3, 4, 10, 12, 13\}$ and $A\cup B=\{1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 14, 15\}$: no number appears in both lists, so the overlap of the two events is $\{\}$ or $\varnothing$.
Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot occur at the same time. With nothing in common, these two cannot, so the answer is yes.
The move that works: ask 'can they occur at the same time?', write out the two events the question names, and look for a number that is in both. If there is none, the events are mutually exclusive.

entries.label: Treats any two complements as mutually exclusive
entries.description: The student knows that an event and its own complement cannot overlap and carries that over to $A'$ and $B'$, which are the complements of two different events, answering 'yes' without checking whether they share a number.
entries.signal: Answers 'yes' (mutually exclusive) when asked about the complements of two different events, for example $A'$ and $B'$.

refutation.text_md: You have hold of something true: an event and its own complement never share a number, so they cannot occur at the same time. The slip is to carry that over to $A'$ and $B'$ just because both have a prime.

That fact only covers an event and its own complement, like $A$ and $A'$. Here $A'$ is everything not in $A$ and $B'$ is everything not in $B$. They are complements of two different events, so nothing keeps them apart.

Check with the sets instead. In the example where $A'=\{2\}$ and $B'=\{2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 12, 13, 15\}$, the number 2 is in neither $A$ nor $B$, so it sits in both complements. The overlap is $\{2\}$, not empty.
Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot occur at the same time. The number 2 shows these two can, so the answer is no.
The move that works: write out both event sets, look for a number that is in both, and say yes only when the overlap is empty ($\{\}$ or $\varnothing$).
